title: How Goldie Swimwear Uses Childhood Nostalgia to Beat the Algorithm
summary: Sisters Rima and Eddy Vaidila bootstrapped Goldie Swimwear from legal-pad sketches to a profitable full-time brand using nostalgia and AI.
body_markdown:
[Goldie Swimwear](https://goldieswimwear.com/) ’s first collection started as sketches on scratch paper. Rima Vaidila and her sister, Eddy, grew up in swimsuits year-round in St. Pete Beach, Florida. In 2018, Los Angeles stores offered them two choices: minimal-coverage styles or gear built for surfers and competitive swimmers. They wanted the fun, playful swimwear of their childhood, so they made it.


For seven years, the sisters grew Goldie without outside funding while holding down other careers. This year, both went full time. Eddy leads creative, social, and influencers, and Rima runs operations.


Here, Rima explains how Goldie plans cash flow around a seasonal business and what to ask a manufacturer before ordering a single sample. She also covers how she uses AI and sales data to make faster inventory decisions.


### On planning fall cash flow around summer sales:


Because we’re a relatively seasonal business, it’s still scary. In the summer, when orders are coming in and it’s all hands on deck, it feels easier. Going into the fall, when it’s slower, definitely feels stressful.


All of our fall cash flow decisions are informed by spring and summer. So we don’t go crazy when it’s busy. We’re not like, “Oh my gosh, we have so many orders. Let’s do these massive photoshoots, these massive activations.” We still need to be scrappy and keep it lean, because we know we have to pay for spring inventory in the fall, when we’re slow.


Over seven years, we’ve finally learned to just relax in the fall. It gives us an opportunity to get things set up for the following year.


### On over-ordering the first collection:


We over-ordered inventory for our first collection. We were super confident in the styles, and we were really excited about having a wider assortment. Looking back now, we should have started a little smaller.


I’m glad we’re delusional, though, because we just figured it out. We were like, “OK, let’s style it in a different way. We’ll do some flat lays. We’ll show different ways to wear it.” It took a while to get through the inventory, but we did, finally.


Sitting on all that stock, we also thought maybe we should go in a different direction. We dabbled in a couple of other prints and styles, and they performed well, but they just didn’t feel like us. We were trying to be this fancy swim brand, and it started to feel like work. So we reeled it back and went all in on our initial concept.


Goldie Swimwear capitalizes on fun designs and bold prints that go beyond what one typically sees in the swimwear industry.


*Goldie Swimwear*


### On cutting photo shoot costs without losing production value:


We felt like we had to do big photo shoots because we were comparing ourselves to massive companies with tons of money to spend. We’re a small, self-funded startup. For our first launch campaign, we booked agency models at super high rates.


Looking back now, we could have done it better, but it’s OK. It’s a good way to spend a lot of money to see if your ideas are good.


We thought that’s what you have to do, but you don’t have to. You can be scrappy. It’s a lot easier now because you can find people on social and teams willing to work within your budget. We do a mix that includes non-agency models who DM us like, “Oh my gosh, would love to shoot with you.” We’ll look at their page and be like, “You’re so cool, and you already wear Goldie. Great, let’s do it.”


### On choosing a factory and asking about MOQs first:


We’d never made swimsuits before. Back then, we were Google searching factories and sending cold emails and WhatsApp messages. Now you can search hashtag manufacturer plus your product on TikTok or Instagram. Founders also share the MOQs they negotiated and what things cost, so you don’t have to do all the groundwork yourself.


We hand-drew our first collection on a legal pad, with no fancy tech packs, and sent the drawings to a couple of manufacturers. We got fabric swatches in person to feel them. Then we compared each manufacturer’s interpretation of our drawings to see who understood what we were going for. With a few of them, we were like, “Yeah, this isn’t right.”


The difference was in the subtle things. Fit is one of the biggest factors in swim: the rise, even the tension of the elasticity.


The factory we loved, unfortunately, had very high MOQs, and looking back now, we probably could have negotiated. Today, that would be my first conversation with any manufacturer, before even sampling. Is this even a road we want to go down? Can we even buy that much? Asking that upfront would have narrowed down our search.


Factories are also more open to smaller orders now than they were in 2018. There’s been a boom in small and online businesses, and factories can see the potential. They’re more willing to do a smaller MOQ just to test it.


Rima and Eddy's brand was inspired by the bold and playful colors of their childhood.


*Goldie Swimwear*


### On the four questions to ask before sampling:


Ask about timeline, sample cost, MOQs, and how many revisions you can get.


Revisions are the part a lot of people don’t think about. We were like, “Yeah, we’ll sample, it’ll be amazing, and we’ll go from there.” Then suddenly your 60-day timeline is no longer what’s happening. Talk through revisions and what the timeline actually looks like, so you don’t get ahead of yourself and plan a launch in 60 days when it’s really not going to happen.


We did three rounds of samples before we got our first collection dialed. Our tried-and-true bestsellers are usually good to go after the first sample. A new style still takes two to three rounds, because we’re crazy about getting our fits right.


### On using AI and sales data to make faster decisions:


There are a lot of AI inventory management tools now that would have been a game changer for us early on, especially once you have historical sales data to look back on. They make it a lot easier to see which sizes and styles are selling through and at what rate. Sales velocity is one of the numbers I check constantly. I look at it weekly for all of our pieces.


I didn’t go to school for finance, so I started using my AI agent to build spreadsheets and pull data that would have taken me hours of manual work. I still double-check everything, but I can make decisions much faster.


For example, I wanted a quote from a potential fulfillment partner. I had my AI agent pull our average shipping weight and average items per order into a spreadsheet. Then I could talk to that partner with specific numbers in mind and get an accurate quote. I also use Sidekick in Shopify all the time to export reports and pull sales data.


Right now I’m digging into returns data on our newer styles. Is something running too small? Does a specific size have a fit issue? We use that to tweak a style, or even to consider dropping it and reworking it.


Creative is the one area we won’t hand to AI. My sister and I love being on set, and we appreciate freelancers and artists. Our nostalgia-driven ethos doesn’t really lend itself to AI.


Goldie Swimwear allows you to mix and match your swimwear.


*Goldie Swimwear*


### On hiring slowly and building systems as needed:


When you’re starting a business, you think you need to hire all these people to do all these jobs. I’m a big believer in fake it till you make it. You can learn on the job. You don’t need to hire a massive C-suite right off the bat.


Hiring slowly is actually the way to go, and that’s how we’ve grown. We’ve stayed bootstrapped and haven’t taken funding. It’s been exciting to grow at a slightly slower pace and make sure it’s profitable.


Systems work the same way for us. We don’t have fancy MBAs, so we build systems as we go. That’s great, because we can build them the way we actually need them, instead of putting big systems in place just because that’s what you’re supposed to do. We’re still figuring it out. Nothing’s ever finished.


For the gifted bikini that sold out a set in a couple of hours, the weird Florida books that keep Goldie off Pinterest, and how Rima and Eddy split the business into separate lanes, watch the full episode on[Shopify Masters](https://www.youtube.com/@shopifymasters) .
